passage: Over the last decade, organizations have increasingly turned to algorithmic management tools to monitor employee performance, assign tasks, and evaluate productivity. From warehouse scanners that track every second of a worker's movement to software that logs keystrokes and mouse clicks for remote staff, digital surveillance has become commonplace across industries. Proponents argue that these data-driven systems boost efficiency, eliminate human bias in evaluations, and allow managers to optimize workflows in real time. However, mounting research suggests that constant algorithmic monitoring often backfires. When workers feel reduced to mere data points under relentless scrutiny, stress and burnout skyrocket while intrinsic motivation and creativity plummet. Moreover, employees frequently adapt by gaming the metrics—prioritizing easily measurable speed over quality, teamwork, or long-term problem-solving. Ultimately, treating human labor as a purely mechanical process undermines the trust and engagement essential for sustainable organizational success.
